summary: A Union Pacific Track Record 101 guide, dated January 18, 2022, that describes the main rail car types and what each carries and how it is built. It covers twelve types, from autoracks and boxcars to tank cars and well cars, and points readers to an infographic and a video. Surrounding navigation, login prompts and unrelated Track Record story teasers are boilerplate and were ignored.
one_line: Union Pacific's Track Record guide explaining twelve rail car types, what each carries, and how each is built.
key_facts: The Union Pacific Track Record article 'What Are All of the Different Rail Car Types?' is dated January 18, 2022 and is categorized under 101.
The guide covers twelve rail car types: autorack, boxcar, centerbeam, covered hopper, coil car, flatcar, gondola, intermodal equipment, refrigerated boxcar, open-top hopper, tank car and well car.
Autoracks are entirely enclosed and typically come as bi-level (two levels, any vehicle type) or tri-level (three levels, usually smaller passenger vehicles).
Boxcars are fully enclosed and typically have doors on the side of the car, protecting freight from weather during transport.
Centerbeams have a 'center beam' or partition that reinforces the center of gravity and allows products to be secured in place.
Covered hoppers have an open top for loading, a sloped floor for gravity unloading through bottom doors, and a top that is covered to protect contents.
Coil cars are designed for coiled steel, steel plate or high-grade ores, and covered coil cars are available when protection from the elements is needed.
Flatcars carry items such as pipe, rail, steel plate, machinery, tractors, military vehicles, lumber, poles and logs, and their open design accommodates oversized and oddly shaped freight.
Gondolas are sturdy cars with low side walls and open tops, described as 'a boxcar cut in half horizontally', and carry heavy bulk commodities such as scrap metal, aggregates, logs and iron ore.
Intermodal containers are described as boxcars without train wheels, and containers can be transferred between ships, trains and trucks without unloading or reloading the cargo.
Open-top hoppers carry coal, petroleum coke, sand, rock and copper concentrate, and differ from covered hoppers in that they have no covers.
Refrigerated boxcars, commonly called 'reefers', are temperature controlled and carry perishable freight such as fresh fruits, vegetables, frozen food, meat and seafood.
Tank cars are more cylindrical than other rail cars and hold between 6,500 gallons and more than 31,000 gallons.
Well cars, also called 'stack cars' or 'well wagons', carry intermodal containers and allow two containers per well car in a 'double stack'.
